title: What we need to live: air, water, food, clothes and a home

summary.text: You take a breath every few seconds, and you never stop. Every person needs air, water and food again and again, because the body keeps using them up. Clothes and a home keep us safe from sun, rain, cold and wind. These five are our basic needs. Your child builds a little wind shelter from a box and finds out which way its open side must face to keep a tissue still in the fan's wind.
summary.art: A child counting on five fingers, with five small pictures around them: a curl of air, a steel tumbler of water, a plate of idli, a cotton shirt and a little house.

intro.hook: Think of a baby, a grandmother and a crow at the window. What does each one need every single day?
intro.text: Say your guesses out loud first. Then count them on your fingers. In this unit we find the five things every person needs: air, water, food, clothes and a home. We find out why we need some of them every few seconds and some only a few times a day. And we build a little home from a box, put it in front of a fan, and test which way its door should face.
intro.art: A baby in a cradle, a grandmother with a steel tumbler, and a crow on a window ledge, each with a small thought bubble showing water, food and a roof.

outcomes: By the end I can name the five basic needs: air, water, food, clothes and a home.
By the end I can say that my body uses up air, water and food, so I need them again and again.
By the end I can say what clothes and a home keep me safe from: sun, rain, cold, wind and insects.
By the end I can show with my wind box that a wall facing the wind makes calm air behind it.
By the end I can say that crows, ants and plants have needs too, and that humans are animals with the same needs.
By the end I can tell how Florence Nightingale counted, and found that clean water and fresh air keep people alive.

terms.meaning: Basic needs are the things every person must have to live and stay well: air, water, food, clothes and a home.
terms.example: A baby, a grandmother and a cricketer all have the same five basic needs.
terms.art: Five round pictures in a row: air, a tumbler of water, a plate of food, a shirt and a house.

terms.meaning: A shelter is a place that keeps you safe from sun, rain, cold and wind. A home is a shelter.
terms.example: When it rains, a bus stop with a roof is a shelter.
terms.art: People standing under the roof of a bus stop while rain falls all around.

terms.meaning: Wind is air that is moving. We cannot see air, but we can see what wind moves.
terms.example: A fan makes a wind. It flaps the pages of a book on the table.
terms.art: A table fan blowing the pages of an open notebook, with soft lines showing the moving air.

terms.meaning: Fresh air is clean air coming in from outside. Used air goes out through windows and doors.
terms.example: Opening the window in the morning lets fresh air into the bedroom.
terms.art: A bedroom window being opened in the morning, with soft lines of air flowing in and out.

explanations.context: This card says what the five basic needs are.
explanations.definition: Basic needs are the five things every person must have to live and stay well: air, water, food, clothes and a home.
explanations.description: Three of them we take inside our bodies: air, water and food. Two of them stay outside us and keep us safe: clothes and a home. Every person on Earth needs all five, wherever they live, rich or poor, young or old.
examples: A newborn baby drinks milk. Milk gives the baby both food and water.
A fisherwoman at sea near Kochi takes drinking water on the boat. Sea water is too salty to drink.
A soldier in the snow of Ladakh needs thick clothes and a warm tent.
explanations.art: A child's open hand with one need drawn on each finger: air, water, food, clothes and a home.

explanations.concept: We need air, water and food again and again
explanations.context: This card explains why we cannot take our needs just once and be done.
explanations.definition: Our body keeps using up air, water and food, so we must take them in again and again.
explanations.description: Your body uses air all the time, so you breathe every few seconds, even in your sleep. Water leaves your body when you wee, sweat and breathe out, so you drink every day. Food gives you the energy to move, grow and stay warm, so you eat a few times a day. A person can live only a few minutes without air, a few days without water, and some weeks without food.
examples: After running, you breathe faster and feel thirsty.
On a hot day in Chennai, you sweat and need more water.
After a long game of kho-kho, you feel hungry.
explanations.art: Three clocks side by side: a breath every few seconds, a tumbler of water a few times a day, a plate of food at breakfast, lunch and dinner.

explanations.concept: Clothes and a home keep us safe
explanations.context: This card explains why clothes and a home are needs, not only nice to have.
explanations.definition: Clothes and a home protect our bodies from sun, rain, cold, wind, insects and dirt.
explanations.description: Your skin can burn in strong sun and get very cold in wind and rain. A cap and loose cotton clothes shade you from the sun. A sweater keeps you warm when it is cold. A home has a roof for rain and sun, and walls for wind. Its doors and windows let fresh air in. A good home is also a safe place to sleep, cook and keep water clean.
examples: Farmers in the fields of Andhra Pradesh often tie a cotton towel on the head against the sun.
In Shillong in winter, people wear woollen shawls and caps.
Houses in rainy Kerala often have sloping roofs, so rain runs off.
explanations.art: A house cut open like a doll's house, with arrows showing rain sliding off the roof, wind stopped by a wall, and fresh air coming in at a window.

explanations.concept: A wall makes calm air behind it
explanations.context: This card explains the wind box test, where a box kept a tissue still.
explanations.definition: When wind meets a wall, the moving air cannot go through, so it flows around and over it. Behind the wall, the air is calm.
explanations.description: In the wind box test, the fan blew air at the box. With the open side facing the fan, wind rushed in and the tissue flapped. With the open side turned away, the closed back wall faced the wind. The air hit that wall and went around the box. Inside, the tissue hung still. So a shelter keeps out the wind best when a wall faces the wind.
examples: On a windy beach, people sit on the side of a boat away from the wind.
Farmers plant rows of trees along the edge of a field, called windbreaks, to slow the wind.
A pigeon sits on the side of a water tank away from the wind.
explanations.art: A box seen from above, with arrows of wind from a fan curving around both sides of the box, and a still tissue flag inside the open side away from the fan.

explanations.concept: Other living beings have needs too
explanations.context: This card is about the needs of crows, ants, plants and other living beings.
explanations.definition: All animals need air, water and food, and many need a shelter. Plants need air, water and light. Humans are animals, so we share these needs.
explanations.description: A crow drinks from a bowl on the balcony on a hot day. Ants carry crumbs back to their nest to feed the young ants. A pigeon builds a nest on a ledge under a roof, out of the rain. A tulsi or money plant in a pot needs water and light. We are one animal among many, and our needs are much the same as theirs.
examples: A cat curls up in a warm, dry corner to sleep.
A crow chooses a shady branch at noon in summer.
Ants hurry their eggs to higher ground before heavy rain.
explanations.art: A balcony with a crow drinking from a steel bowl, a line of ants carrying crumbs, a pigeon on a ledge and a tulsi plant in a pot.

agreed.text: Every person needs air, water and food to stay alive, and clothes and a home to stay safe and well.
agreed.evidence: Doctors everywhere agree. People who go without air, water or food become ill quickly and can die.

agreed.text: Air is needed soonest, then water, then food.
agreed.evidence: A person can live only a few minutes without air, a few days without water, and some weeks without food.

agreed.text: Wind flows around a wall and leaves calmer air behind it.
agreed.evidence: You saw it in the wind box test. Farmers see it too: the plants just behind a row of trees are sheltered from strong wind.

challenging.claim: A home must be shut on every side to keep out the wind.
challenging.who: A common guess, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Shutting the doors and windows does stop the wind.
challenging.against: In the wind box test, the box with its open side away from the fan kept the tissue still. A wall facing the wind is what matters most.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that only a shut home keeps the wind out.

challenging.claim: Food is the need we must have soonest.
challenging.who: A common guess among young children
challenging.for: We feel hungry many times a day, and food fills us up.
challenging.against: A person can live some weeks without food, but only a few minutes without air. We need air soonest of all.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that food is the most urgent need.

big_questions.q: The wind went around the wind box. Where did it go after that?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the fan's air ends up in the room.

big_questions.q: Why do we breathe all the time, but eat only a few times a day?
big_questions.hint: Think about which one your body uses up fastest.

big_questions.q: Is love a need, like food and water? What would happen to a baby who had food but no one to hold them?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gives a baby their food and water.

big_questions.q: A pigeon, an ant and you all need a home. Is a home a thing, or a safe place?
big_questions.hint: Think about the pigeon behind the water tank in the story.

story.title: The Tent on the Terrace
story.note: Lasya, Kiran, Amma and Ammamma are made up. Visakhapatnam is a real port city on the coast of Andhra Pradesh. Wind really does flow around a wall and leave calmer air behind it.
text: Lasya lived in a flat in Visakhapatnam, a big city by the sea. She was seven. Her little brother Kiran was five. On top of their building was a wide, flat roof called the terrace.
One warm evening in the holidays, Ammamma said, "Let us eat our dinner on the terrace tonight. We will make a little home up there."
Lasya and Kiran carried up two plastic chairs and an old bedsheet. Amma carried a steel bottle of water and a box of lemon rice. Ammamma brought her soft cotton shawl.
On the terrace, the wind was blowing hard from the sea. It flapped Lasya's frock and lifted Kiran's hair straight up.
Ammamma put the two chairs back to back, a little apart. She spread the bedsheet over them and tucked it in. Now it was a tent, with three sides closed and one side open for a door.
"Our house!" said Kiran. He crawled in with the box of lemon rice.
But the open door of the tent faced the sea. The wind rushed straight in. The bedsheet puffed up like a balloon. A paper plate flew out of the tent and rolled away across the terrace.
"My plate!" shouted Kiran. Lasya ran after the plate and caught it beside the big water tank.
Behind the water tank, the air was calm. Lasya's frock hung still. A grey pigeon sat there on a ledge, with her feathers smooth and tidy. Just one step away, the wind was still blowing hard.
Lasya stood still and thought. The wind was coming from the sea. The tank stood between her and the sea. So the wind hit the tank and went around the sides.
"Ammamma!" she called. "The pigeon has found a calm place. Look, behind the tank, on the side away from the sea."
Ammamma smiled. "Then what should we do with our tent?"
"Turn it round!" said Lasya. "Put the door away from the sea. Then the closed back will face the wind, like the tank."
Together they turned the chairs round. Now the closed back of the tent faced the sea, and the open door faced the town.
Lasya crawled in. The bedsheet was quiet. The paper plates lay still. Outside, the wind still whistled past, but inside the tent the air was calm.
Kiran looked at the open door. "But the door is open," he said. "Why doesn't the wind come in?"
"The wind hits the back wall," said Lasya. "Then it goes around the sides, past the door. The pigeon knew that before we did."
They sat inside and ate the lemon rice. They drank cool water from the steel bottle. When the sea wind turned cooler, Ammamma wrapped her cotton shawl around Kiran's shoulders.
Kiran counted on his fingers. "We have air to breathe. Water to drink. Rice to eat. A shawl to wear. And a home." He held up five fingers. "Five things!"
"Those are the five things every person needs," said Ammamma. "Air, water, food, clothes and a home. People everywhere need them, every day."
"Does the pigeon need them too?" asked Kiran.
"She needs air, water and food, just like us," said Lasya. "Her feathers are her clothes. And behind the tank is her shelter tonight."
Kiran thought about this. Then he filled the steel lid of the water bottle and set it down near the tank, for the pigeon.
Later, the stars came out over the sea. The pigeon was still on her calm ledge. And three people sat in their calm little tent, with the door wide open.
story.epiphany: Lasya finds calm air behind the water tank, on the side away from the sea wind, where a pigeon is sitting. She turns the tent so its closed back faces the wind, and the tent goes calm even with the door open.
ask: Why did the wind rush into the tent at first?
How did the pigeon help Lasya?
What five things did Kiran count on his fingers?
art: A bedsheet tent on a city terrace puffed up like a balloon in the sea wind, with a paper plate flying out and a small boy reaching after it.
A girl standing behind a big water tank on a terrace, looking at a calm grey pigeon on a ledge, with wind lines curving around the tank.
Two children and their grandmother eating lemon rice inside a calm bedsheet tent at dusk, the open door facing the city lights.

games.title: Five Needs, Ten Helpers: a matching game
games.context: This is a card game about the five basic needs. Five need cards lie face up. You pick helper cards and put each one under the need it gives you.

items.b: We breathe air in every few seconds.
We drink water every day.
Food gives us energy to move, grow and stay warm.
Clothes keep our skin safe from sun, cold and insects.
A home keeps us safe from rain, sun, cold and wind.
Air. It lets fresh air into the room.
Air. You breathe in through your nose.
Water. You drink it.
Water. It keeps drinking water cool and covered.

items.f: A plate of idli and sambar
items.b: Food. It gives you energy.
Food. Fruit gives you energy, and some water too.
Clothes. It keeps the rain off your body.
Clothes. It keeps you warm on a cold night.
A home. It keeps off the rain and the hot sun.

items.f: A pigeon's nest on a ledge
items.b: A home. It is the pigeon's shelter.

rules: Lay the 5 need cards face up in a row.
Mix the 10 helper cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Pick the top helper card and read it out.
Put it under the need it gives you. Say why.
Turn it over to check. If it is in the wrong place, talk about it and move it.
When all 10 are placed, say which need you could go without for the shortest time.

setup.art: Five cards face up in a row on a mat: Air, Water, Food, Clothes, A home.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the five need cards in a row.

setup.art: A child placing a card showing a clay matka under the Water card.
setup.caption: 2. Pick a helper card. Put it under the need it gives.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 15 cards. 2. Lay the 5 need cards face up in a row. 3. Mix the helper cards face down.
flow.say: These five cards are the five things every person needs. These other cards are helpers. Each helper gives us one need.
flow.kid: These are the five needs. The other cards are helpers. Each helper gives one need.

flow.do: Take turns picking a helper card. Read it aloud. Ask for a reason before it goes down.
flow.say: Which need does this one give us? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Which need does it give? Say why.

ask.q: Which need does the open window give?
good: Fresh air comes in through it.

flow.parent: The pigeon's nest is a good one to talk about. A nest is a home for a pigeon. Humans and other animals both need shelter.

flow.do: When all cards are placed, ask the last question.
flow.say: Look at the five needs. Which one could you go without for the shortest time?
flow.kid: Which need do you need soonest?

check.q: Which need do we need soonest?
check.why: We need air every few seconds. Without air, a person lives only a few minutes. We can go some weeks without food.

games.title: Weather Comes! Run to the right shelter
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller shows a weather card. Everyone runs to the right shelter, or puts on the right clothes.

items.b: Get under a roof. Crawl under the table.
Get behind a wall. Crouch behind the sofa, on the side away from the fan.
Get into the shade. Put a cap or a towel on your head.
Wrap up in a shawl or a bedsheet.
Pull your sleeves down to your wrists.
Pretend to drink a tumbler of water.

rules: Choose one caller. The caller holds the 6 weather cards.
The caller shows a card and reads it out.
Everyone runs to the right shelter, or does the right action.
The caller reads the back of the card to check.
Then a new player becomes the caller.

setup.art: A living room with a table, a sofa, a table fan in one corner and a shawl on a chair.
setup.caption: 1. Find a table, a sofa, a shawl and a cap before you start.

setup.art: Two children crouching behind a sofa on the side away from a table fan, while a woman holds up a card saying Wind!
setup.caption: 2. The caller shows a card. Run to the right shelter.

flow.do: 1. Switch the fan on. 2. Put a shawl and a cap on a chair. 3. Show everyone the table and the sofa.
flow.say: When I show a card, run to the right shelter. The table is our roof. The sofa is our wall.
flow.kid: The table is a roof. The sofa is a wall. Listen for the weather!

flow.do: Show the cards one at a time, in any order. Check with the back of each card.
flow.say: Wind! Where will you hide? Which side of the sofa is the calm side?
flow.kid: Run to the right shelter. Do the right action.

ask.q: Why did you hide on that side of the sofa?
good: It is away from the fan.
The sofa stops the wind there.

flow.parent: Keep the running gentle indoors. Push sharp corners and glass out of the way first.

flow.do: Ask one last question.
flow.say: Which cards needed a roof, and which needed a wall?
flow.kid: Which weather needs a roof? Which needs a wall?

experiments.title: The Wind Box: which way should the door face?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a wind with a fan and a little flag of tissue that shows where the wind is. Then you build shelters from a cardboard box and find which one keeps the flag still.
experiments.question: A box has a roof, walls and one open side, like a door. To keep a tissue flag still inside, should the open side face the fan or face away from it? And does a tunnel, open at both ends, keep the wind out?
experiments.predict: Guess first. In which shelter will the tissue flag stay still: the tunnel, the box with its door to the fan, or the box with its door away from the fan? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The fan stays at the same speed and the same place, about two big steps from the box. The tissue flag stands in the middle of the box each time. Only the shelter changes.
results_table: What the tissue flag did: flapped, wobbled, or hung still

materials.item: a table fan or a pedestal fan (no table fan: a grown-up waves a big book or a tray hard, from one side)
a cardboard carton at least as tall as a ruler, like a delivery box
a tissue or a paper napkin
a small steel tumbler full of rice or dal, to hold the pencil upright
paper and crayons, for the results

experiments.safety: Keep fingers, hair and the tissue away from the fan blades. A grown-up does the cutting and moves the fan.

schedule.what: Make the tissue flag. Test it in the open, in a tunnel, and in a box with its door to the fan and then away from it.

experiments.record: Draw the box and the fan for each test. Draw the tissue flying for 'flapped' and hanging straight down for 'still'.

setup.art: A thin strip of tissue taped to the top of a pencil, standing upright in a small steel tumbler full of rice.
setup.caption: 1. Make a tissue flag. Stand the pencil in a tumbler of rice.

setup.art: A cardboard carton lying on its side with both ends open like a tunnel, a tissue flag inside, and a table fan two steps away blowing straight through.
setup.caption: 2. Test a tunnel, open at both ends.

setup.art: The same carton with the back end taped shut and the open side turned away from the fan, and the tissue flag inside hanging still.
setup.caption: 3. Close one end. Test the door facing the fan, then facing away.

flow.do: 1. Tear a strip of tissue, two fingers wide and as long as your hand. 2. Tape its top end to the top of the pencil. 3. Stand the pencil upright in the tumbler of rice.
flow.say: This is our wind flag. It will show us where the wind is. When the air moves, the tissue moves.
flow.kid: Make a tissue flag. It shows you where the wind is.
flow.parent: Tissue works best because it is so light. A strip from a thin plastic carry bag also works.

flow.do: 1. Switch the fan on to medium. 2. Put the flag on the floor or a low table, two big steps in front of the fan.
flow.say: Watch the flag. What is moving it? We cannot see the air, but we can see what it does.
flow.kid: Watch the flag. What is moving it?

ask.q: What is making the flag move?

flow.do: 1. Lay the carton on its side. 2. A grown-up opens or cuts the bottom so both ends are open, like a tunnel. 3. Show your child the tunnel and the tape. 4. Ask for guesses.
flow.say: Soon this tunnel will become a box with one door. Which shelter will keep the flag still? Should the door face the fan, or face away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which shelter will keep the flag still? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where should the door face? Why?
good: Away from the fan, so the wind can't get in.
Towards the fan, so I can see in.

flow.parent: Write down the guess and the reason. Any reason is a good start. Do not say which is right yet.

flow.do: 1. Put the tunnel over the flag, so the fan blows straight through one end and out of the other. 2. Watch the flag for a slow count of ten.
flow.say: The flag has a roof and two walls now. Watch it. Does it flap, wobble or hang still?
flow.kid: Your flag has a roof now. Does it still flap?

ask.q: Did the tunnel keep the wind out?
good: No, the wind blew straight through.

flow.do: 1. Lift the carton off. 2. Tape one end shut, so the box has one open door. 3. Put it back over the flag with the door facing the fan. 4. Watch for a slow count of ten.
flow.say: Now the box has one door, and the door faces the fan. Watch the flag.
flow.kid: Now the door faces the fan. Watch the flag.

good: It wobbled, because wind came in through the door.

flow.parent: The flag may flap hard or only wobble, depending on the size of the box. Either is fine. Compare it with the next test.

flow.do: 1. Lift the box and turn it round, so the closed end faces the fan. 2. Put it back over the flag in the same place. 3. Watch for a slow count of ten.
flow.say: Now the closed wall faces the fan, and the door faces away. Watch the flag. What do you see?
flow.kid: Now the wall faces the fan. What does the flag do?

ask.q: What did the flag do now?

flow.parent: The flag should hang still or barely move. If it still flaps, check that the fan is blowing at the closed end, and move the flag deeper inside the box.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me what you found out. Which way should a door face on a windy day? What did the flag show you? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Which way should the door face? What did your flag show you?

check.q: In which test did the tissue flag hang still?
options: The tunnel, open at both ends
The box, door facing the fan
The box, door facing away from the fan
check.why: With the door facing away, the closed wall faced the fan. The moving air hit that wall and went around the box, so the air inside stayed calm.

flow.parent: A strong answer: I think the door should face away from the wind. The flag hung still when the wall faced the fan. The wind hit the wall and went around.

activities.title: Five Needs on Five Fingers
activities.context: In this activity you meet each of the five basic needs with your body: a breath, a sip, a bite, a touch of your clothes and a touch of your wall.

materials.item: a small piece of food, such as a raisin, a peanut or a piece of banana

schedule.what: Meet each need with your body, one finger at a time.

activities.record: Draw your hand. Draw one need on each finger.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged, taking a slow breath with one finger raised.
setup.caption: 1. Thumb: take a slow breath. Index finger: take a sip of water.

setup.art: A child touching the sleeve of their cotton shirt, then putting a palm flat on the wall of the room.
setup.caption: 2. Touch your clothes. Then touch the wall of your home.

flow.do: 1. Hold up your thumb and take one slow breath together. 2. Hold up the next finger and take a sip of water. 3. Hold up the middle finger and eat the small piece of food.
flow.say: Every person needs five things. Here are three of them. Breathe in air. Sip water. Eat a little food. Where did each one go?
flow.kid: Take a slow breath. Sip some water. Eat a little food. Where did they go?

ask.q: Where did the air, water and food go?

flow.do: 1. Hold up the fourth finger and touch your clothes. 2. Hold up the little finger and press a palm on the wall of the room.
flow.say: Here are the last two. Touch your clothes. Touch the wall of our home. Did these go inside you?
flow.kid: Touch your clothes. Touch the wall. Did they go inside you?

ask.q: How are clothes and a home different from air, water and food?

flow.do: Ask the last question. Wait for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Which of these five do you need again soonest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which one do you need again soonest? Why?

ask.q: Which do you need again soonest?
good: Air, because I breathe all the time.
Air. I need another breath in a few seconds.

flow.parent: Children often say food. Let your child hold their breath for a moment if they like, then breathe. That answers it.

activities.title: Find the Calm Spots at Home
activities.context: In this activity you carry your tissue flag from the wind box test around a room with the fan on. You find the calm spots, where walls and furniture keep the wind away.

materials.item: the tissue flag from the wind box test
3 small paper stars or bits of paper, to mark calm spots

schedule.what: With the fan on, carry the flag round the room and mark the calm spots.

activities.record: Draw a map of the room. Draw the fan, and a star on each calm spot.

setup.art: A child walking slowly across a living room holding a tissue flag on a pencil, with a ceiling fan turning above.
setup.caption: 1. Switch on the fan. Walk slowly with your flag.

setup.art: The tissue flag hanging still behind a sofa, with a paper star on the floor beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Where the flag hangs still, put a star.

flow.do: 1. Switch on the fan. 2. Your child holds the flag at knee height and walks slowly round the room. 3. Put a paper star wherever the flag hangs still.
flow.say: Let's find the calm spots in this room. Hold your flag low. Where does it hang still?
flow.kid: Walk slowly with your flag. Where does it hang still?

good: The sofa is in the way of the wind.

flow.parent: With a ceiling fan, the wind blows down and out. Calm spots are often under a table, behind a sofa or beside a cupboard.

flow.do: Look at all the stars together.
flow.say: Look at our stars. What is next to each calm spot?
flow.kid: What is next to each star?

ask.q: What do the calm spots have in common?
good: They are behind a wall or a sofa.

activities.title: When I Was a Baby: what did I need?
activities.context: In this activity you look at baby photos of yourself with a grown-up. You find out how each of the five needs was given to you before you could do anything for yourself.

materials.item: a few baby photos of your child, printed or on a phone

schedule.what: Look at baby photos and talk about how each need was met.

activities.record: Draw yourself as a baby, and draw who gave you each need.

setup.art: A mother and a child looking at baby photos on a phone together.
setup.caption: 1. Look at your baby photos together.

setup.art: A baby in a cloth cradle hanging from the ceiling, with a woman nearby holding a small steel tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Find each need in the photos: food, clothes, a home.

flow.do: Look at the photos together. For each one, find the needs you can see.
flow.say: Here you are as a baby. Who gave you your food? Who kept you warm? Where did you sleep?
flow.kid: Look at baby you. Who gave you food? Where did you sleep?

ask.q: How did you get food and water as a baby?

flow.parent: Tell your child one true thing about their baby days: what they drank, a favourite cloth, where they slept. Milk gives a baby both food and water.

flow.do: Ask the big question, and listen.
flow.say: A baby cannot get any of the five needs alone. So what else does a baby need?
flow.kid: What else does a baby need?

ask.q: What else does a baby need?

projects.title: Our Bedsheet Home: a tent with all five needs
projects.context: In this project you build a tent from chairs and a bedsheet, like Lasya in the story. You turn its door away from the fan's wind and bring all five needs inside.

materials.item: an old bedsheet or a dupatta
the tissue flag from the wind box test

projects.safety: Use light chairs, and keep the tent away from the fan blades and the stove.

schedule.what: Build the tent, test it with the flag, then bring in all five needs and eat a snack inside.

projects.record: Draw your tent from outside, with the fan, and draw the five needs inside.

setup.art: Two chairs placed back to back with a bedsheet spread over them to make a tent, with one open side.
setup.caption: 1. Put two chairs back to back. Spread the sheet over them.

setup.art: A child sitting in a bedsheet tent with a water bottle, a small plate of snacks and a shawl, the open door facing away from a table fan.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the door away from the fan. Bring in the five needs.

flow.do: 1. Put two chairs back to back, a little apart. 2. Spread the bedsheet over them. 3. Tuck it in so three sides are closed and one side is open.
flow.say: Let's build a home, like Lasya's tent on the terrace. Where should the door go?
flow.kid: Build a tent with chairs and a sheet. Where will the door go?

flow.do: 1. Switch on the fan. 2. Put the tissue flag inside. 3. Turn the tent so the door faces the fan, then away from it.
flow.say: Let's test our tent with the flag. Which way keeps it calm inside?
flow.kid: Put your flag inside. Turn the tent. When is it calm inside?

ask.q: Which way keeps the tent calm?
good: The closed side facing the wind.

flow.do: Bring in the water, the snack and the shawl. Sit inside together and eat the snack.
flow.say: Now let's bring in all five needs. Count them on your fingers as we go.
flow.kid: Bring in water, food and a shawl. Count your five needs.

ask.q: Where is the air in our tent?

flow.parent: Air is the one children forget. Point out that the tent is full of it, and fresh air comes in through the open door.

challenges.title: A Home for the Tissue Flag, Wind From Any Side
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Build a shelter that keeps the tissue flag still, even when the fan is moved to blow from a different side.
challenges.problem: A real home stands in one place, but the wind can come from any side. Build a shelter for your tissue flag that keeps it still when the fan blows from the front, then from the side.
constraints: Use only things from home: books, card, paper, a box or cloth.
The flag must hang still for a slow count of ten.
A grown-up moves the fan to a new side after the first test.
materials: the tissue flag from the wind box test
books, card or a cardboard box
a table fan or a hand fan
general: Close all four sides and leave a small door you can shut.
Make the door face away from the wind, and turn the shelter when the wind changes.
creative: Build a round wall that curls like a snail shell, so the door is tucked inside the curl.
Hang a cloth curtain over the door, so wind from any side cannot rush straight in.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own shelter. Draw it, build it, and test it with the fan from two sides. What would you change?

setup.art: A child building a small shelter of books standing on their edges around a tissue flag, with a table fan behind.
setup.caption: 1. Build a shelter around your flag.

setup.art: A grown-up moving the table fan to the side of the shelter while the child watches the flag.
setup.caption: 2. Move the fan to a new side. Is the flag still calm?

flow.do: Show your child the problem. Look at the flag in the open fan wind first.
flow.say: Real wind can blow from any side. Can you build a home that keeps our flag calm, whichever way the wind blows?
flow.kid: Build a home for your flag. The wind may come from any side.

flow.do: Your child chooses an idea, or invents one, and builds the shelter.
flow.say: Which idea will you try? Where will the door go?
flow.kid: Choose an idea. Build your shelter.
flow.parent: Help with tape if needed, but let your child choose the shape.

flow.do: 1. Test with the fan in front. 2. Then move the fan to one side and test again.
flow.say: Watch the flag. Now the wind comes from the side. What happens?
flow.kid: Test it. Now the wind comes from the side. Is it still calm?

good: Close the door when the wind changes.
Make the wall go all the way round.

videos.check: Find a real, accurate video for age 6 and add its id. Check it says the deaths fell after the drains and water were cleaned in 1855, and does not say she did it alone.

videos.why: Shows moving air curving around a wall and a calm patch behind it, like the wind box test.
videos.check: Find a real wind tunnel or smoke film and add its id. Check it shows the calm area behind the object.

quiz.p: Which of these is one of the five basic needs?
quiz.why: Water is a basic need. A toy car and a phone are nice to have, but we can live without them.

quiz.p: Which need do we take in every few seconds?
quiz.why: We breathe air every few seconds, even in our sleep. We eat food only a few times a day.

quiz.p: Why do we drink water every day, and not just once?
opts: Water leaves our body when we wee, sweat and breathe out
quiz.why: Our body keeps losing water, so we must keep putting it back.

quiz.p: What does a roof keep off us?
quiz.why: A roof keeps off the rain and the hot sun. Walls keep off the wind.

quiz.p: Remember the wind box test? Where should the open door of the box face, to keep the tissue flag still?
quiz.why: With the door away from the fan, the closed wall faced the wind. The air went around the box, so the flag hung still.

quiz.p: In the wind box test, a tunnel was open at both ends. What did the tissue flag do inside it?
opts: It flapped, because the wind blew straight through
It hung still, because it had a roof
quiz.why: A roof alone does not stop the wind. The wind blew in at one end and out of the other.

quiz.p: Which of these is a shelter for a pigeon?
opts: A nest on a ledge under a roof
quiz.why: A nest under a roof keeps a pigeon safe from rain and wind. It is the pigeon's home.

opts: Humans are animals, and we need air, water and food like other animals
quiz.why: Humans are animals. Crows, cats, ants and people all need air, water and food. Plants need air, water and light.

quiz.p: What did Florence Nightingale find when she counted the soldiers in her hospital?
opts: Most were dying of illness from dirty water and drains, not of wounds
Most were dying because they had no toys
quiz.why: Her counts showed far more soldiers dying of illness than of wounds. When the drains and water were cleaned, far fewer died.

quiz.p: Malini, a girl in Madurai, goes out in the hot sun in May. What should she wear?
opts: A cap and loose cotton clothes
quiz.why: A cap shades her head, and loose cotton lets sweat dry and keeps her cool.

items.p: Draw a line from each need to the thing that gives it.
items.why: Each thing gives us one need. A window lets in fresh air, and a roof keeps us safe from rain.
items.art: Five needs on the left, and five pictures on the right: a window, a matka, a dosa, a raincoat and a roof.

items.p: Draw your hand. Draw one basic need on each finger.
items.a: Air, water, food, clothes and a home, one on each finger.
items.why: A strong drawing shows all five needs. Any order is fine.
items.art: The outline of a child's hand with five empty fingers.

items.p: Circle the needs we take inside our body. Put a box round the needs that stay outside and keep us safe.
items.why: We breathe in air, drink water and eat food. Clothes and a home stay outside us and protect us.
items.art: Five small pictures: air, water, food, a shirt and a house.

items.p: Remember the wind box test? The door of the box faced away from the fan. What did the tissue flag inside do?
items.why: The closed wall faced the fan, so the wind went around the box. The air inside was calm.

items.p: Draw the fan and the box with its door facing away. Draw the tissue flag inside.
items.a: The fan points at the closed end. The flag inside hangs straight down.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the closed wall facing the fan, and the flag hanging still.
items.art: An empty box on the page with a small table fan drawn at one side.

items.p: We need air only when we are running.
items.why: False. We breathe all the time, even when we sit still and when we sleep. We breathe faster when we run.

items.p: Which one is NOT a basic need?
items.why: A video game is fun, but we can live without it. Water, food and a home are needs.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why do you drink water every day?
items.a: My body keeps losing water when I wee, sweat and breathe out. So I must drink more.
items.why: A strong answer says the body uses up or loses water, so it must be put back again and again.

items.p: Here is a house. Write R next to the part that keeps off the rain, W next to the part that stops the wind, and A next to the part that lets in fresh air.
items.a: R on the roof, W on a wall, A on a window.
items.why: A roof keeps off rain and sun, walls stop the wind, and windows let fresh air in.
items.art: A simple house with a sloping roof, walls, a door and an open window, with three empty boxes.

items.p: A crow comes to a bowl on the balcony on a hot day. Which need is the crow meeting?
items.why: The crow is thirsty, like us on a hot day. Crows need water too.

items.p: Two friends in Kolkata are building a tent on a windy terrace.

views.says: Put the door towards the wind, so the fresh air comes in.
Put the door away from the wind, so the tent stays calm.

items.ask: Who will have a calmer tent? Use what you saw in the wind box test. Then say one thing the other friend got right.
items.a: Joy will have a calmer tent, because the closed back faces the wind. But Rumi is right that a home needs fresh air. A tent with its door away from the wind still gets fresh air through the door.
items.why: A strong answer uses the wind box test and is fair to Rumi: fresh air is a need too.

items.p: Remember the tunnel in the wind box test? It had a roof but was open at both ends. What does this tell us?
opts: A roof alone does not stop the wind
A roof always stops the wind
items.why: In the tunnel, the flag flapped. Wind blows from the side, so we need a wall facing it.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why did the flag hang still when the box's closed wall faced the fan?
items.a: The wind hit the closed wall and went around the box. So the air inside stayed calm.
items.why: A strong answer says the wind went around the wall, not through it.

items.p: Put these in order, from the need we must have soonest to the one we can go without for longest.
items.why: A person lives only a few minutes without air, a few days without water, and some weeks without food.
items.art: Three pictures: a plate of food, a curl of air, a tumbler of water.

items.p: Sunita lives in Shimla. In January it is very cold. Which clothes does she need?
opts: A woollen sweater, a cap and socks
items.why: Wool keeps her warm. In Chennai in May she would need loose cotton instead. The need is the same, but the clothes depend on the place.

items.p: Draw a home for a pigeon. Show what keeps off the rain and the wind.
items.a: A nest on a ledge under a roof, or in a corner with a wall on the windy side.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a roof for rain and a wall against the wind. Pigeons choose such places in our buildings.

items.p: Plants need nothing to live.
items.why: False. Plants need water, air and light. A plant in a pot droops if nobody waters them.

items.p: Fill the gap: Wind is air that is ____.
items.why: Wind is moving air. We cannot see it, but we see what it moves, like the tissue flag.

items.p: Here is the wind box from above, with a fan on one side. Draw arrows to show where the wind goes. Put a C where the air is calm.
items.a: Arrows curve around both sides of the box. The C is inside the box, near the door.
items.why: A strong answer shows the wind going around the closed wall, and the calm air inside.
items.art: A box seen from above with an open side away from a small fan.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: a baby has milk, clothes and a cradle. What else does a baby need, and why?
items.a: A baby needs someone to look after them, because a baby cannot get food or water alone.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a baby depends on other people for every need. Many doctors say care and love are needs too.

applications: Farmers plant rows of trees along the edge of a field, called windbreaks, to slow the wind and protect the crops.
Campers put up a tent with its door facing away from the wind.
On the coasts of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, strong cyclone shelters are built so that families can stay safe in big storms.
After a flood, relief teams bring the basic needs first: drinking water, food, clothes and tents.
Homes, schools and hospitals are built with windows, so fresh air can come in.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a pigeon or an ant find the calmest, safest spot?
open_questions.why_open: Animals sense wind, warmth and wet in many ways. Scientists are still finding out how each animal chooses a shelter.

open_questions.q: How much water does each person really need in a day?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the heat, the person and the food they eat. Doctors still argue about exact amounts. The rule of eight glasses for everyone is not based on strong evidence.

open_questions.q: Is sleep a basic need, like food and water?
open_questions.why_open: Every animal studied so far sleeps or rests. Scientists still argue about all the things sleep does for the body.

ask_kids: What did you need first when you woke up this morning?
Where is the calm side of our building on a windy day?
What does the crow at the window need today?
Which of your clothes keep off the sun, and which keep you warm?
What does our home keep out?

jokes.j: Why did the tissue flag hide behind the box?
jokes.a: It wanted a little peace and quiet!

jokes.j: What did the roof say to the rain?
Why do we breathe so often?
jokes.a: Because we can't save it up for later!

jokes.j: What did the water say to the thirsty child?
jokes.a: Drink me, I'm a need, not a want!

jokes.j: Why did the wind go around the house?
jokes.a: The door was facing the other way!

jokes.j: What kind of house does a snail need?
jokes.a: None. She carries it on her back!

jokes.j: Why did the idli go to school?
What did one wall say to the other wall?
Why did the sweater stay home in Chennai in May?
jokes.a: It was too hot to go out!

maths.problem: In the wind box test, Priya tried 4 shelters. The tissue flag flapped in 3 of them. In how many did it hang still?
maths.answer: 1 shelter. The flag hung still only in the box with its door facing away from the fan.
maths.explain: 4 shelters take away the 3 where the flag flapped leaves 1.
maths.context: This is about the wind box test, where a tissue flag showed if wind got in.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the shelters that failed tells us how many worked.

maths.problem: Kiran counts his needs on his fingers: air, water, food, clothes and a home. His sister Lasya counts hers too. How many fingers do they hold up together?
maths.answer: 10 fingers. Each of them has 5 needs, and 5 and 5 make 10.
maths.explain: 5 needs for Kiran and 5 for Lasya. 5 add 5 is 10. Every person has the same five needs.
maths.context: This is about the five basic needs, counted on fingers as in the story.
maths.why_maths: Adding shows that every person brings the same five needs, so more people need more of each.

maths.problem: Meena drinks 2 tumblers of water in the morning, 2 at lunch and 1 in the evening. Make a tally mark for each tumbler. How many tumblers did she drink?
maths.answer: 5 tumblers. The tally is 2, then 2, then 1, which makes 5 marks.
maths.explain: 2 add 2 is 4. 4 add 1 is 5. On a hot day she may need more.
maths.context: This is about why we drink water again and again through the day.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows how many times in one day we put back the water our body loses.

founder: ideas/by_topic/basic-needs.md was read. Its concept activity is about sound under water and does not fit this topic, so it was not used. Its SCI Cards (Alice Ball, Barry Marshall, Aditi Pant, M. S. Swaminathan, Varahamihira) do not match a Class 1 shelter unit and were left for other units.
No board chapter is listed for this level. The level 3 unit (sci.basic-needs.basic-needs.L3) was read so that this unit leads into it without repeating its tests, story or deep truth.
science: Flow around a bluff body: wind meeting a wall or box flows around and over it, leaving a sheltered region of slower, calmer air on the far side. This is the basis of shelterbelts and windbreaks in farming.
Survival without air (minutes), water (days) and food (weeks) are standard rough figures used in medicine and first aid.

Florence Nightingale took 38 nurses to the British army hospital at Scutari in late 1854. The Sanitary Commission cleaned the drains and water supply from March 1855, and deaths fell sharply. Her diagrams were published in 1858. She studied army and village health in India through reports, without visiting India. She held the miasma idea, that bad smells carry illness.
Florence Nightingale, Notes on Nursing, 1859: the first rule of nursing is to keep the air the patient breathes as pure as the air outside.

roots.context: We have found that a box kept a tissue flag still when its closed wall faced the fan. Now we ask what that tells us about homes, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: With its open side turned away from the fan, the box kept the tissue still. The moving air hit the back wall and flowed around the box. Behind that wall the air stayed calm. So a home can keep out the wind even with an open door, if a wall faces the wind.
deep_truth.habit: We think a shelter keeps us safe only when it is shut on every side, like a box with a lid. In the test, one wall on the windy side made calm air behind it. Which way a wall faces matters as much as how many walls there are.
deep_truth.evidence: In the wind box test, the tissue flag flapped in a tunnel open at both ends, and flapped or wobbled with the box's door facing the fan. With the same box turned round, door away from the fan, the flag hung still.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal who needs air, water and food every day, just like a crow or a cat.
three.what_is_life: Being alive means taking in air, water and food again and again, and keeping safe while you do.
three.what_is_this_world: The same air flows over every home on Earth. Every shelter is a calm place the moving air goes around.

roots.thread: The air that moves as wind is the same air we breathe. A wall does not take that air away. It turns the air aside and makes a small calm place behind it. A pigeon chooses that calm place behind a water tank, and a family chooses it when they build a home. One air flows around all of us, and every shelter is shaped by it.

teachings.teaching: We cut out doors and windows to make a room. It is the empty space inside that makes the room useful.
teachings.link: In the wind box, the box gave the tissue flag a calm space. The walls and the door were useful because of the space they made inside.

teachings.teaching: Food is the source of life. From food beings are born, by food they live, and into food they go back.
teachings.link: We need food again and again, because our body keeps using it to live and grow.

teachings.teaching: Rain keeps the world alive, so rain is called the nectar that gives life.
teachings.link: Every person, crow and plant needs water. The water in our taps and wells came first as rain.

science.text: Wind flows around a wall or a row of trees and leaves calmer air behind it. Farmers use windbreaks for this.
How a pigeon or an ant senses and chooses the safest, calmest spot is still being studied.

other_view.view: Many scientists say a pigeon on a calm ledge is not choosing. They say the bird simply moves until the wind stops pushing on her feathers, the way a ball rolls into a dip.

practice.title: Be a wall for your breath
practice.say: Hold one hand up in front of your face, a little away. Blow gently on it. Can you feel your breath? Now hold your other hand in between, like a wall. Blow again. Can the back hand feel your breath now? Where did your breath go? Sit still and feel the calm air behind your wall.
practice.kid: Hold up one hand. Blow on it. Now put your other hand in front, like a wall. Blow again. Where did your breath go?

ask: When the wind goes around your home, where does it go next?
In the story, the pigeon sat behind the water tank. How do you think she knew where the calm air was?
Is a home the walls, or the calm space the walls make?
roots.art: A child holding one hand in front of the other and blowing gently, with soft lines of breath curving around the front hand.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that clean water and fresh air keep people alive? This card tells a true story.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1854, Britain was fighting a war near the Black Sea. Florence Nightingale, a nurse from England, went with 38 nurses to a big army hospital at Scutari, in Turkey. The hospital was crowded and dirty. The drains were blocked, the water was not clean, and the wards smelled bad. Most people thought the soldiers were dying of their wounds. Florence and her nurses kept careful counts, every day. Their numbers showed something else. Far more soldiers were dying of illnesses, like cholera and typhus, than of wounds. In March 1855, a team came from Britain to clean the drains and the water supply. After that, far fewer soldiers died. Florence drew coloured pictures of her numbers, so that everyone could see. For the rest of her life she worked for clean water, fresh air and clean homes, in Britain and in India too.
how_we_found_out.who: Florence Nightingale, a nurse from England, her nurses, and the Sanitary Commission sent from Britain
how_we_found_out.when: 1854 to 1855 at Scutari. Her diagrams were published in 1858.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most people thought the soldiers died mainly of their wounds. The counts showed that far more died of illness from dirty water and blocked drains. Florence, like many people then, also thought illness spread through bad smells. Later scientists found that germs, for example in dirty water, spread it.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman in a long dress and white cap holding a lamp, writing numbers in a notebook beside rows of beds in a long hospital ward.
